#2754. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

Frank Cappelleri is the founder and president of CappThesis, an independent research firm that helps active investors through time-tested chart and statistical analysis. Prior to starting CappThesis, he spent 25 years on Wall Street as an equity sales trader, technical analyst, research sales specialist and desk strategist.

#2753. Trump Account contributions from friends and family pass $1 billion mark, Treasury says

Families and friends have collectively contributed more than $1 billion to Trump Accounts since the July 4 launch, bringing total deposits to more than $9 billion, the U.S. Department of the Treasury said Tuesday in an announcement exclusively provided to CNBC.

The $1 billion in Trump Account deposits come from more than 3 million individuals, according to the agency. That total does not include the government's seed money or philanthropic gifts from donors such as Michael and Susan Dell.

"The American people are investing in Trump Accounts with a generosity that represents the finest instincts of our national character," U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a written statement.

"Trump Accounts are a transformative government program for American children. It is the largest government start-up in American history," Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano said in the statement.

Also known as 530A accounts, Trump Accounts are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.

Parents, guardians, grandparents and others can collectively contribute up to $5,000 per child per year in after-tax dollars up until the year before the beneficiary turns 18. The annual contribution limit is indexed for inflation after 2027.

Children born from 2025 through 2028 may receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria.

Most recently, Snowflake chairman Frank Slootman and his wife, Brenda, announced they would give $1,000 to every child in Montana born in 2023 and 2024.

The Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold stock donations, a move meant to pave the way for more philanthropic gifts, according to Bisignano.

These rules make it more attractive for donors, according to Ben Henry-Moreland, a certified financial planner with advisor platform Kitces.com.

By gifting stocks, wealthy founders and shareholders can avoid the capital gains taxes that would otherwise be triggered by selling appreciated stock and donating the cash proceeds. However, it also means some children's wealth accumulation could be tied to the performance of individual companies.

The Trump Accounts milestone comes as more billionaires and companies pledge support to the investment account for kids.

In an exclusive interview with CNBC's "Squawk on the Street," Bessent on Nov. 20 announced an Anthropic co-founder would make a "large gift" to Trump Accounts over the next few weeks.

A person briefed on the announcement confirmed that the Anthropic co-founder Bessent referred to is Tom Brown and that it is part of his broader philanthropic plan. The person asked not to be named because the matter is private.

"This is the perfect vehicle to donate to the children of America, and they will receive 100% of the proceeds," Bessent said.

Elon Musk wrote in an X post that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX sometime in 2027, which experts say may come via Trump Accounts.

In a separate funding announcement, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said she would donate around 2 million shares of her and her husband's SpaceX stock to the accounts.

On Monday, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, founder of Invest America and an architect of Trump Accounts, told CNBC's "Halftime Report" that more large-scale donations may be in the pipeline.

"I want everybody to own shares of Nvidia, in Anthropic, in OpenAI," he said. "We created 70 million stock accounts — free stock accounts — for every single citizen under the age of 18 to do just that, and we have huge announcements coming."

#2751. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

#2750. Utah drops criminal charges against Kalshi founders after company suspended operations in state

Utah on Tuesday dismissed criminal charges against Kalshi and its two co-founders following the decision by the prediction market platform on Monday to suspend operations in the state.

The state originally filed the 14 criminal charges against the company and founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara on Oct. 28, claiming that Kalshi operated an illegal gambling operation in the state.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets which views itself as the sole body that can develop rules over the growing industry — sued Utah the day before the state announced its charges.

Mansour and Lara were slated to appear in a Utah district court on Dec. 4, according to court documents.

However, Kalshi suspended operations in Utah on Monday, citing legal uncertainty. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown celebrated the decision in a statement announcing the move to dismiss the state's charges.

"Every company in this space should take note," he said. "If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable."

Brown's office noted in the statement that dismissal is without prejudice, meaning if Kalshi were to begin operations again in the state the charges could be refiled.

"Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized," Kalshi's general counsel Yaakov Roth said in a post on X. "We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets."

While Kalshi faces legal setbacks in Utah, it faced some relief in New York on Monday when a state judge denied an emergency temporary restraining order against the company to halt its operations in the jurisdiction. The court will hear arguments on the matter again in January.

#2749. 30 things to be thankful for in the NBA, including Victor Wembanyama's greatness and the Lakers' chemistry

As we approach the 20-game mark in the NBA's regular season, I must say it's been a true joy to watch these teams compete — trying to learn what they're good at, where they struggle and adjusting on the fly. They may not have all the answers quite yet, but the effort is there. It can be easy to sit back and criticize, but ultimately it's more fulfilling to lead with gratitude. Here are 30 things I'm thankful for.

East: Atlanta Hawks • Boston Celtics • Brooklyn Nets • Charlotte Hornets • Chicago Bulls • Cleveland Cavaliers • Detroit Pistons • Indiana Pacers • Miami Heat • Milwaukee Bucks • New York Knicks • Orlando Magic • Philadelphia 76ers • Toronto Raptors • Washington Wizards

West: Dallas Mavericks • Denver Nuggets • Golden State Warriors • Houston Rockets • LA Clippers • Los Angeles Lakers • Memphis Grizzlies • Minnesota Timberwolves • New Orleans Pelicans • Oklahoma City Thunder • Phoenix Suns • Portland Trail Blazers • Sacramento Kings • San Antonio Spurs • Utah Jazz

(Dillon Minshall/Yahoo Sports Illustration)

The month of November. Last year at this time, the Hawks went 10-5 with the ninth-best defensive rating in the league. So far this month they are 8-2 with the fifth-best defensive rating. Having a new level of wing depth thanks to the additions of Aaron Wiggins and Lu Dort has allowed them to balance different lineups through injuries. When the Hawks' defensive activity (see Daniels, Dyson) keeps opponents out of the paint, they get a chance to run and flow.

Their defense. Poor timing (like a recent four-game losing streak) can put a damper on things this time of year, but the Celtics have rarely had to worry about that on the defensive end of the floor. They have consistently defended as a unit, showing early help, swarming on any sort of dribble penetration and working to dictate terms on what types of shots they give up. This will be key as they navigate more and more teams working to trap Jayson Tatum on offense.

Thankfully, this is only the second time in 10 regular seasons that the Nets have started 3-13 (don't ask me how I know). Then again, this is now back-to-back seasons where they have started 3-13, with opponents scoring 129 or more points against them in five of their last seven games. If they can string together some stops, it may feel different. OK, on a brighter note, their broadcast team is elite and the ABA court is fire.

Who doesn't appreciate something that didn't look so fun on paper and then suddenly did? Look at the turnaround from the Bulls, who have found a balance offensively and some effort defensively. Buddy Hield has made 18 3s in his last four games! Nic Claxton is switching (again). Tiago Splitter is unafraid to expand his rotation and stick to what's working out there.

Sometimes reality, an honest conversation and a look in the mirror can be what you need. That's what the Hornets have received as their offense has plummeted and their defense has not held up to the pressure. Kon Knueppel has played only six minutes this season and the Hornets did start 4-12 last year before making a play-in run, so perhaps brighter days are ahead.

Sometimes the leftovers are better than the initial meal. Cleveland's record and consistency are likely not where it thought it would be after last year's deep run. But the moments where you see how much James Harden and Donovan Mitchell impact a game and how the Cavs' bench provides them a different type of energy means there could be a deeper payoff down the line.

Morez Johnson Jr.'s start. Sure, there is a consistency that Cooper Flagg is playing with and an ease that Kyrie Irving displays that sets up shots for everyone to contribute, but let's recognize the energy that Johnson brings to the table and the potential he has on the defensive end of the floor. Weakside communication and rotations should not be ignored, folks.

Their adaptability and understanding how to get the job done. The Nuggets have turned their season around by winning 9 out of 13 games and it feels like they are working to find ways to win different types of games — trusting a level of versatility whether it's an offensive shootout or their defense is getting stops. It also very much helps that Jamal Murray and Nikola Jokić are always at the table.

Their evolution continues to stand out. More movement, more flow, quicker decisions. They will have to find balance and avoid old habits, but continuing to move Ausar Thompson around the board before Jalen Duren returns is a good thing. Cade Cunningham, who sat out Tuesday with knee soreness, has continued to cook no matter who has been in the lineup.

It's Stephen Curry. The Warriors should be thankful they have Stephen Curry — who is averaging 27.8 points per game and shooting 45.7% from 3 at 38 years old — and hope he returns to the court as soon as possible.

The wisdom Fred VanVleet and Marcus Smart have delivered in spades. VanVleet, in particular, just has a way of making the exact play the Rockets need over and over again. He reads defenses to open things up, and makes them pay with shots when they anticipate the pass. Smart's ability to defend multiple positions puts everyone else in a more comfortable spot.

The uncompromising nature in which the Pacers play the game of basketball. No matter who is in the lineup, if shots are falling, if they are getting stops: they are going to work to play Pacers basketball. The ball is going to move, the drives are going to be there, the passes will persist. It might be Andrew Nembhard eating up space, Ivica Zubac making an impact in the paint or Pascal Siakam doing a little bit of everything. They don't stop. Just watch Kelly Oubre.

Brandon Ingram's return. Is there a chance that the talent on the Clippers can finally come together and maximize their ability to be bothersome in the Western Conference? Hope goes a long way, and the more scoring and playmaking the Clippers can have on the court the better. Darius Garland has been game, but the Clippers just need to sustain the good they find rather than reinvent the wheel.

The chemistry that has elevated the Lakers. Luka Dončić has been lights out, but the build around him has continued to pay off. They can get to multiple lineups and get consistent production up and down the roster. You never quite know who could help break a game open for them. Every night you can feel them attempting to accomplish the same goals on each end.

Internal growth. As tremendous as Ty Jerome and Cameron Boozer have been, has anyone been paying attention to the development from Cedric Coward and Cam Spencer? Coward hit 33.8% of his 3s last year and is shooting 44.7% from 3 this year while attempting more of them. Spencer continuously makes plays (and shots) within the flow of what the Grizzlies want to do. They are a team that believes in what they do every night and the internal growth shows it game in and game out.

Davion Mitchell, who has done everything this team has asked him to do and more. The defense speaks for itself, but the playmaking has grown. Mitchell is unafraid to direct the offense, he's reading defenses better, and his paint touches mean more. Mix in some shot-making and he's as happy as Klay Thompson running an empty-side action. Coach Spo has (once again) expanded his menu by mixing in pick-and-rolls or post-ups when needed, too.

Not all charcuterie boards are the same, but you can find the right combinations, even in the wildest ones. Brayden Burries' drives have been fun, but there is a rhythm that is helping him find consistency on the court. Him playing well while Tyler Herro gets all of the buckets is a positive sign. Herro scoring 50 and 32 in back-to-back games while shooting 60%+ from the field is not easy, either.

Consistency. It's not hard to see these Wolves play the game with a level of joy, but they also bring a level of steadiness, particularly on the defensive end. Rudy Gobert patrols the paint, but their ability to use their size and length to switch and bog teams down continues to ignite their transition attack. The fact that they can have this level of lineup consistency on both ends of the floor speaks to a different world in Minnesota.

The growth of Zion Williamson. It's been an up-and-down time in New Orleans, but that shouldn't take away from the Pelicans star's performance. The team has been more willing to switch him defensively and he's worked to hold up. The drives remain, but there's an ease to get to a short pull-up. He's even mixed in 3s on occasion. Tack on the consistent drives from Jeremiah Fears and there is still some potential on this plate.

Every single dish, dunk and drive from Karl-Anthony Towns this season. If last year was about KAT answering questions, this year has been about him delivering problems. The Knicks have been able to lean more into playing through him, opening their offense for everyone. He's also found the gaps to attack, making it tough on bigs and working to punish wings who switch. It also means you really don't know when and where Jalen Brunson is going to attack.

Trusting in your principles in the face of adversity. The Thunder know what they want to work toward and trust they can get there, but each night brings a different test as they navigate injuries. Lineups that used to be a strength (double big/small ball) may present new challenges with this group.

Franz Wagner playmaking. Sometimes you're asked to handle more responsibility or you graduate to a different table this time of year. Since Oct. 30, Wagner has six games where he has 10 or more assists. Prior to that he had done it only two times in his career. It's not just reading defenses, it's bending defenses and understanding what his move can do to force a defense to react. Positive sign for the Magic.

The ability to figure things out and adjust on the fly is always something to be thankful for. It's been a big reason why the Sixers have been able to climb to the top of the Eastern Conference. It may not be the ideal setting, but what in life is? Led by Tyrese Maxey, they are 12-0 in clutch games this season while shooting 50% from the field and 52% from 3 before they have everything figured out. That is a good sign.

Getting back to the basics. Success is not always linear, and just because you do something well once does not mean it will automatically transfer. Returning to the basics of what Phoenix likes to do defensively should help soften some of its offensive issues. It's always good to be self-aware in these moments. It helps that the Suns are 6-2 when Collin Gillespie scores 10 or more points.

Who doesn't love a good homecoming? The Damian Lillard return continues to pay off as the Blazers are able to get the most out of him without putting the total weight of the offense on him. And who doesn't love a good wing? Toumani Camara is a mad man, Sidy Cissoko has continued to defend multiple positions … and they are both making 3s?

It's the ground floor of the Darius Acuff Jr. Experience, and while the wins may not be there right now … sometimes you're in the building for something special before it truly becomes that. Whether it's the straight-line drives, the ability to get to his own shot when he wants or the reps to develop his playmaking, there is a payoff here.

Being able to watch Victor Wembanyama play basketball every single night. There is a moment in almost every game that feels like it's something you've never witnessed before. Criticism is fair, but greatness shouldn't be ignored.

Again, who doesn't appreciate a good wing? Toronto has them in bunches and they all deliver in different ways. The growing comfort of Scottie Barnes when it comes to getting to his shot in the midrange. Collin Murray-Boyles' ability to be everywhere at once on any given possession. Allen Graves and his quick hands; best of luck if you overpenetrate around him.

Opportunities for Darryn Peterson to grow. Injuries have taken their toll on this Jazz roster and the fact that 15 of their 19 games played have been against teams at .500 or above has not helped. But there have been plenty of chances for Peterson to develop as a playmaker and a defender. A lot of the issues feel controllable: the up-and-down ball movement, inconsistent defense and turnovers. You have to hope it gets better, but as Will Hardy said, hope is not a strategy.

Before Monday's loss to the Celtics, the Wizards had not just won three straight games, but had held three straight opponents to sub-100 points scoring. For the season, they have held opponents under 100 five times. They did it three times last year. Effort goes a long way.

#2748. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2746. Dell earnings beat on AI strength, company authorizes $25 billion buyback

Dell reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that topped Wall Street expectations for earnings and sales, and provided a strong guide for the fourth quarter.

Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates:

Dell said that it expected earnings of $8.40 per share on revenue of about $56.3 billion in the current quarter. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $7.50 per share on $53.61 billion in revenue.

The company's overall sales more than doubled on an annual basis during the third quarter, driven by AI server demand.

The company's largest line is its infrastructure solutions group, or ISG, which makes AI servers and systems, often based around AI chips from companies like Nvidia and AMD.

ISG sales during the quarter were $41.97 billion, topping an LSEG estimate of $35.27 billion. Of that, $22 billion was for AI-optimized servers, up 291% on an annual basis. ISG now accounts for 85% of Dell's total revenue.

"We are now a different company, with Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of our profit and growth," said Jeff Clarke, Dell's vice chairman and COO, in a statement. He said that Dell has 7,500 customers buying AI servers.

In prepared remarks, Clarke said that Dell has a competitive advantage over other computer equipment makers because it allows customers to get their computers working within hours of delivery.

"That allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably," Clarke said in the prepared remarks published by Dell.

The company also raised its forecast for AI-servers in the coming fiscal year to $78 billion, versus $74 billion expected. The company says it has a backlog of $132.3 billion in AI server orders it is working through.

"Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power," Clarke said on an earnings call with analysts.

The company also sells laptops and PCs, in a group it calls CSG, or client services group. It reported $12.89 billion in sales, which was below LSEG expectations of $14.33 billion.

The overall PC market has been getting whacked of late, with some estimates calling the lull the worst ever, as rising memory prices have led to higher device prices and consumers are choosing to hang on to their old laptops longer.

Dell said that it had authorized $25 billion in share repurchases, and that it had spent $4.9 billion in the third quarter on share repurchases and dividends.

Dell shares are up over 135% so far in 2026.

#2745. Nets vs. Bucks preview: Brooklyn looks to end five-game losing streak

MILWAUKEE, WISCONSIN – NOVEMBER 15: Tyler Herro #11 of the Milwaukee Bucks runs down court during the first half of the game against the Atlanta Hawks at Fiserv Forum on November 15, 2026 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Bad basketball teams find ways to lose games. On Monday night, the Brooklyn Nets tied the game against the Minnesota Timberwolves at five early in the first quarter. And that was the closest they got. Brooklyn never led and trailed by as much as 30 points on national TV. They lost by 26 points, 142-116, withe the losing streak sitting at five entering Wednesday's matchup against the 2-16 Milwaukee Bucks.

They've had their fair share of struggles this year.

The Bucks are at the bottom of the NBA standings, but they had a good time in Canada on Monday night. They took on the Toronto Raptors and won 116-111. The win snapped their 13-game losing streak, which was the second-longest in franchise history. You take the wins where you can get them.

Matchup: Brooklyn Nets (3-13) vs. Milwaukee Bucks (2-16)

By the numbers, these are the two worst defensive teams in the NBA. Brooklyn allows 120.3 points per 100 possessions, worst in the NBA. Milwaukee isn't that far behind at 119.8 points per 100 possessions — the second-worst in the NBA. These two teams allow easy buckets and bad defense makes games a lot harder to sit through if you're rooting for the team with the bad defense.

Look for this one to be a high scoring affair and whoever can put together enough stops on defense should walk away with the win.

Where the Nets have doomed themselves this year is in the turnover department. Brooklyn commits the second most turnovers in the league this year and when you combine that with a bad defense, it explains why this team is in the mud.

If the Nets want to start putting wins together, they're going to need real play out of Michael Porter Jr. MPJ tied a season low in field goal attempts with seven on Monday night and was virtually non-existent out there. It's not easy when the team is in a rut, but as one of the vets on the team and a former NBA champion, more is expected of MPJ. He's admittedly trying to find his rhythm, and tonight would be a good time to find the right mix heading into a weekend back-to-back.

Myles Turner is another one of those players you forget has been in the league a long time. This is his 12th season in the league and he figures to be a trade candidate this winter. In theory, Turner provides floor spacing, rim protection, and deep postseason experience for any teams out there in the market. The Raptors are certainly looking for help at the five and if they ever get fully healthy, maybe Turner is the player that pushes them over the top.

Herro was the centerpiece of the trade that sent Giannis Antetokounmpo to the Miami Heat, and Bucks management is looking to see how he fits into their future plans. From Dalton Sell at Behind the Bucks Pass:

"With each passing game, it's becoming clearer that Brayden Burries and Kasparas Jakucionis need as much playing time as possible. Just 21 and 20 years old, they are oozing the type of potential that could make them the franchise's backcourt for the next decade plus. It's hard to let them entirely off the leash when players like Herro are commanding so many minutes, though.

If the Milwaukee Bucks truly believe in these two, it would make sense to move Herro and potentially even other guards like Ryan Rollins to unleash the duo. It wouldn't hurt to collect assets as well. The Bucks should be on the hunt for future draft picks and young players, and if someone offers a solid combination of those things, it would make trading Tyler Herro that much easier to stomach."

We'll see. Herro has been on a hot streak of late as he's shot above 50% from the field in three consecutive games.

Mikel Brown Jr got his first start of the season, and he'll get all the minutes he can handle now that Nolan Traore is out for the next few months. Brown Jr. looked good in his time out there against the Wolves with 17 points, and we'll see if the Nets let him play 30 minutes amid an early-season minutes restriction. Brown Jr's development is the only thing that is preventing Nets fans online from staging a full-on revolt at this point.

Even as the losses pile up for Brooklyn, Brown Jr playing well would at least give a sense of hope that things are heading in the right direction. The next step is leading the Nets in a win they should get.

Grand Theft Auto VI has taken over the world and the game looks absolutely sensational. With that in mind, let's revisit some of my favorite missions from a previous era of GTA.

#2744. AI debt worries grow as Nvidia rebound masks Big Tech spending squeeze

Big Tech could find it increasingly tough to secure funding from debt markets critical to the AI build-out, as lenders become pickier over corporate bonds.

Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO on Monday gave an already-rising stock market a further lift, with tech shares leading a broad rebound on Wall Street after last week's sharp sell-off as Anthropic's landmark IPO failed to lift the broader sector.

But investors are now starting to ask harder questions about the bill for the AI build-out — and demanding evidence that the huge spending is actually adding value for shareholders, according to Dan Taylor, deputy chief investment officer and CIO equities, systematic at Man Group.

"As investors get choosier about where all this capital is going and when it might pay off, we think the market is likely to fragment well beyond the simple 'buy chipmakers, sell software' trade of the past two years," Taylor said.

"Anthropic may have got its IPO out the door just in time, but for the rest of the AI trade, the era of spending first and asking questions later seems to be over."

Anthropic — which went public Nov. 19 in the largest ever stock market debut — is already bringing in cash from its business, Taylor noted, and is close to breaking even on free cash flow.

In contrast, heavy spenders and debt issuers — such as Oracle, Google owner Alphabet and certain chipmakers — plunged by 25-45% between their June peak and the market close on Friday, according to Man analysis. By comparison, Apple, which has sat out the AI spending arms race, was up almost 20%, Taylor observed in a Man Group note Tuesday.

Nvidia closed about 5.9% lower on Tuesday. Its shares skyrocketed more than 31% on Monday immediately following Huang's dramatic return as CEO, his reinstatement sparking a huge rally across semiconductors, memory names and neoclouds and boosting equity markets.

Matthew Rees, head of global bond strategies at L&G Asset Management, acknowledged bond markets have been consistently more bearish on Big Tech hyperscalers than equity markets. That stems partly from debt investors' broader outlook on the sector, but also from the sheer volume of issuance, Rees said.

"You're seeing BBB names like Oracle and SpaceX that are trading more like single B, partly because of concerns over fundamental credit quality, but also very much concerns about supply," Rees told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" Tuesday.

Accelerated AI-related borrowing is becoming a bigger share of U.S. corporate debt. PIMCO, citing Goldman Sachs data, expects the biggest AI companies to tap about $250 billion through bond sales this year. Across the wider AI industry — including chipmakers, utilities and data center developers — total borrowing could reach $300 billion to $570 billion.

Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are now on track to spend more on capital projects than their businesses generated in cash in both 2026 and 2027, according to Man Group analysis. Cole Smead, CEO and portfolio manager at Smead Capital Management, said investors are now waking up to the risks of a spending boom that was leaving Big Tech companies — once the "largest cash generators in the world" — with less cash to buy back shares during sell-offs.

"There are vast capital needs in this AI story. The only problem is there's just not enough money to go around," Smead said.

He also questioned whether investors buying data center debt were being paid enough for the risks they were taking.

"They think they're getting 200-300 basis points over 10-year Treasury," Smead told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" before Huang returned on Monday.

"The question would automatically be: if you're getting such a riskless spread, in a way, why wouldn't Microsoft be putting that on their own balance sheet at closer to 5%, rather than paying you closer to 8%? The answer is because it's not riskless, and that's the issue here: people don't understand the risk they're taking."

Looking ahead, Taylor said the past week has demonstrated that a mega-IPO like Anthropic no longer lifts the whole market.

"We think the mega-cap tech spenders have room to rebound, yet doing so will likely require them to show more spending discipline and rebuild their free cash flow," Taylor said. "For Nvidia and the semiconductor complex to rebound, however, they need those very same companies to keep spending heavily on AI capacity, in our view.

"It is hard to see how both sides get what they need at the same time."

#2743. Joe Brady can become the fifth coach ever to win 10 of his first 11 games

Buffalo's Joe Brady is off to one of the best starts for any head coach in NFL history.

The Bills are 9-1, which means that if they beat the Chiefs on Thanksgiving night, Brady will be just the fifth coach in NFL history to win 10 of his first 11 games.

The four who have done it before are Jim Caldwell (11-0 with the 2009 Colts), Wally Lemm (who went 9-0 as interim head coach of the 1961 Houston Oilers and then won one of his first two games after becoming head coach of the 1962 St. Louis Cardinals), Steve Mariucci (10-1 with the 1997 49ers) and Red Miller (10-1 with the 1977 Broncos).

Brady took over a good Bills team and has kept them near the top of the NFL. His record to start his head-coaching career is impressive, but he was brought in to win in the postseason, and so it's too soon to say whether the Bills' decision to fire Sean McDermott and replace him with Brady will pay off.

#2741. Houthi attack on Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund PIF's tower injures 11

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis hit Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund Public Investment Fund Tower on Tuesday, injuring 11.

The kingdom's civil defense directorate did not name the tower, but posted an image showing damage to the PIF tower. Eyewitness reports by Al Jazeera also indicated that the building that was hit was the PIF Tower in Riyadh.

The injured included two Saudi citizens, two Indians, three Nepalis, and four Egyptians.

The attack comes as tensions have flared up again between Saudi Arabia, which is leading an international coalition to restore the internationally recognized government of Yemen after it was forced to flee in 2015, and the Houthis.

Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the coalition, said one of the towers of the financial center was targeted in a "cowardly terrorist attack," referring to the financial center in the Saudi capital of Riyadh.

He added that authorities were conducting an on-site investigation at the scene of the attack.

This has been the second attack by the Iran-backed group in six days on the tower, although the previous attack did not cause any casualties.

On Wednesday, Houthi brigadier general Yahya Saree warned on X that the port of Jeddah and all Saudi ports along the Red Sea coast will become "targets for our forces," if Riyadh attacks the Yemeni Red Sea port of Hodeidah.

The coalition had asked civilians to evacuate the port "for their safety," on Nov. 20.

Attacks by the rebel Houthis have been escalating on Saudi Arabia, with the group targeting one of Saudi Arabia's oil refineries on Sunday, according to Reuters. The Houthis also launched drone and ballistic missiles against the country's airports, most recently targeting the King Khalid International Airport on Oct. 25, according to reports.

The new attacks come amid wider strikes by Tehran and Iran-linked forces in the Gulf, with Bahrain also reporting that it was attacked by Iran over the weekend. Bahrain is home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet.

"As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site," Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said on X.

The ministry later said two people, a Bahraini citizen and a Pakistani resident, were injured in the attack.

— CNBC's Azhar Sukri contributed to this report.

#2740. Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers

Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers' five-game winning streak was snapped Monday night by the Trail Blazers.

With a 128-111 defeat at Xfinity Mobile Arena, the Sixers dropped their first game of the year against Western Conference opposition and fell to 14-4. Portland improved to 11-6.

LeBron James had a season-high 23 points and six rebounds. Tyrese Maxey scored 22 points and Jaylen Brown added 20.

Deni Avdija led the Blazers with 31 points and seven assists. Donovan Clingan posted 15 points and 18 rebounds.

The Sixers were missing Joel Embiid (illness). Ja Morant (left hamstring strain) and Shaedon Sharpe (right knee meniscus surgery) were among Portland's sidelined players.

Next on the Sixers' schedule is a Wednesday night game vs. the Heat. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Blazers:

Jabari Walker, listed at 6-foot-7, defied conventional wisdom by winning the opening tip-off against the 7-2 Cllingan. Maxey then canned a three-pointer.

Brown scored the Sixers' next four points with a pair of free throws and a short jumper. VJ Edgecombe's layup gave the team a 9-2 lead. Brown and Dean Wade both returned Monday after sitting out the last two games with left hamstring injuries.

Avdija got hot in the first quarter. He scored 11 quick points, made his first four field goals and helped the Blazers avoid a serious early deficit.

The Sixers took a 32-30 edge with 9.3 seconds left in the first when Walker jammed in a put-back dunk. The former Portland second-round draft pick played 17 minutes in his second start of the season and continued to look deserving of a rotation spot. He posted 10 points and five rebounds.

Adem Bona was available again following an eight-game absence with a cervical spine sprain. However, Dominick Barlow checked in first to back up Walker.

Barlow had an outstanding start to his night. He scored a clever lefty push shot over Clingan and threw down a dunk in the first quarter. Barlow also made a highlight defensive play in his opening stint, defending Avdija in isolation and rejecting his layup attempt.

Bona then subbed in for Barlow with 3:23 left in the first quarter. He had a positive first possession, grabbing an offensive rebound and driving in for a dunk.

Wade later played at center, too. Barlow logged 16 minutes and had six points. Bona recorded four points and two boards in five minutes. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse ended up using a 10-man rotation and did not play rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. until fourth-quarter garbage time.

Overall, the Sixers' defense remained considerably worse without Embiid. The team also conceded 15 offensive rebounds, including five to Clingan.

"I think your rim protection and ability to do that with some size is always a focal point of being really good defensively," Nurse said. "And then you've got to do it a little bit by committee (with Embiid out). I thought, for the most part, I was looking at possessions where I liked our help into the paint. They were doing a good job of zinging it out.

"I didn't particularly like our (defense) back out. … There were a couple of times they missed those and still got rebounds. We were compacted in the lane with everybody because we didn't get back out, and then still giving up an offensive rebound as well. That's just playing through the possession, a little bit of energy, all that kind of stuff. … We just didn't do enough pieces well."

Brown delivered tons of efficient offense for the Sixers in the first half and sure didn't appear rusty. His layup late in the second quarter tied the game at 58-all. The five-time All-Star scored 19 first-half points on 8-for-10 shooting.

Avdija exceeded Brown's production, hitting heat-check threes, leaners through contact and just about everything he put up regardless of the defender. He tallied 25 points in the first half and shot 9 for 12 from the field.

James reached 16 points when he capped a high-scoring half by nailing a corner three. The contest was even at 69 apiece heading into halftime.

Monday's game was James' first of the season with three or more made three-pointers. The four-time MVP went 4 for 5 beyond the arc. He'd gone 10 for 46 (21.7 percent) over his first 13 games and was due for a good long-range night.

James was whistled for his third foul early in the third quarter. Brown picked up his fourth with 10:15 to go in the period, forcing him to sit for an extended stretch.

"I wasn't too happy about it. … I think that affected the game," Brown said. "It also affected my rhythm a little bit in the second half. I had to sit (almost) the whole third quarter. Coming back from injury, coming back from a hamstring thing, my body didn't really feel the same after that."

Brown noted postgame that he had "a little bit of soreness and stuff like that."

"I think everything will check out," he said. "The medical staff is on top of everything. Those hamstrings are tricky, so you want to make sure you play it the right way, be safe. I also don't want to miss a lot of games, so I might be out there, but I've also got to be smart. I think I played it the right way today."

Avdija stopped lighting up the Sixers in the third period, but the team still had another unimpressive defensive quarter. Portland posted 32 points in the third and built its lead to double figures in the opening minute of the fourth.

The game devolved into a blowout. An Avdija dunk put the Blazers' advantage at 22 points with 5:15 on the clock and the Sixers didn't have a miracle comeback in store.

Even with all their wins, there's no question the Sixers have been trending downward on defense over the past couple of weeks, allowing regular dribble penetration and plenty of comfortable threes.

They'll aim to raise their level on that side of the floor and expect Embiid's presence to be a major help once he's back in action.

"I think it's just mindset," Walker said. "We're capable when we want to. You need games like this every now and then just to remind you that it's not as easy as it feels sometimes. It takes effort every game.

"I think we can learn a lot from this. It's just part of the growing pains, but I'm confident we'll get back to that (early-season) level of defense. We have what it takes."

#2738. There are 5,100 newly minted Anthropic millionaires — here’s all the stuff they don’t tell you about when you suddenly get rich

Things are about to get very weird for the thousands of employees of Anthropic who just became, or soon will become, multimillionaires.

Anthropic's IPO on Nov. 19 turned around 5,100 nonfounder "Ants," as the company's staffers are known, into "paper millionaires," and at least 400 will be worth north of $100 million.

Few of us will ever make a million-dollar windfall from an employer. And fewer still will win the lottery or magically land a massive sum from an estranged rich uncle. But don't be too jealous of these employees' gains. Sure, money can buy a lot — and it would be hard to say no if you do strike it rich — but there are a remarkable number of downsides to sudden wealth.

And they may explain why you likely won't see all of Anthropic's newly minted millionaire employees heading for the exits.

First of all, these new moguls won't be able to access all their wealth immediately. The terms of the stock sale outlined in Anthropic's revised S-1 allow employees to cash out up to 10% of the value of their holdings on the first day of trading following the date of the prospectus, but the rest can only be exercised after various vesting periods pass or lock-up terms are achieved, based on the individual's agreements with the company.

Some won't be able to realize all their gains for years. There are many financial institutions willing to lend based on paper gains, or to buy options — but their wealth will also continue to fluctuate with the rise and fall of the company's stock price.

Even after those riches become liquid, research shows that only a small but still significant percentage of employees will leave as a direct result of their new wealth. No, they aren't jetting off to the South Pacific to board their new yacht — which is what I would do in my "I just got $10 million" fantasy. Instead, according to a 2017 study from the Federal Reserve, an estimated 17.5% of employees at a newly public company will use their newfound wealth as a financial cushion to join another pre-IPO startup or form another company.

These departures, the study finds, may be particularly painful for Anthropic since the most valuable and entrepreneurially minded employees tend to bolt for this reason.

Experts who deal with suddenly wealthy employees expect that many will keep on working because they love it. "They're successful people in their own right," said David Rust, a financial advisor and co-founder of wealth management firm Quartz Financial in Austin, Texas.

Rust said that of his firm's high-tech employee clients who get sudden IPO wealth, "very few just go play golf every day. They want to stay busy and active, and a lot of them will scale back depending on their age, but very few of them say, 'OK, I'm done with that.'"

Others will keep working because their payout wasn't life-changing, said Susan Bradley, a certified financial planner and founder of The Sudden Money Institute, a Palm Beach Gardens, Florida-based financial advisory firm that specializes in clients undergoing sudden wealth events.

That's especially true for those whose millions measure in the low single digits. "You can go through $2 million pretty quickly in the world we live in," said Bradley.

A sum north of $1 million might seem life-changing to most of America, but it's chump change in Anthropic's headquarters city of San Francisco, the fifth most expensive city in the United States, with nearby San Jose coming in at third, according to a Q3 2026 Cost of Living report from Council on Community and Economic Research, which tracks metro- and state-level economic data.

In 2025, the Bay Area had the second-highest number of people with a net worth of $100 million or more of any major metro in the world, according to a study by New World Wealth, a market research firm, in conjunction with Henley & Partners, a global residency and citizenship planning firm. That ranking is sure to get a boost from Anthropic's IPO.

Those who stay at Anthropic may be in for a bumpy ride. A study published in July in Management Science by two researchers from the University of Oklahoma found that employee satisfaction generally tends to crater after an IPO, especially among the earliest employees who had the biggest IPO payday.

The study found that the primary reason for this dissatisfaction is that the rules change when a company is public, and the free-wheeling startup energy, decision-making and risk-taking can be dampened by shareholders and SEC rules.

Plus, imagine trying to get an employee base of 96% newly minted millionaires to continue to work super-duper hard. That's bound to cause some intracompany friction, especially if you are a manager who didn't get a big payout.

Another important matter that I don't game out in my $10 million fantasy, and the Anthropic millionaires probably didn't either, is how strange their friends, family and significant others are about to get. What would you do if your husband, girlfriend, sister or best friend was suddenly the richest person you'd ever met in your life?

Those relationships are going to change and not necessarily for the better, said Paul Hokemeyer, a licensed marriage and family therapist and author of "Fragile Power: Why Having Everything is Never Enough." Think of all the times the new millionaires are going to face someone with their hand out, many of whom will be related to them by blood or marriage.

"In my practice, I see a dynamic where the person of wealth gives out of a place of generosity," said Hokemeyer, "and in short order their acts of largesse create unhealthy dependencies and entitlement. Then, when the giver decides to stop or pull back, the recipient becomes a victim and the giver a perpetrator." He advises his clients to make no personal or charitable financial gifts for six months to a year, and not until they've created a specific giving plan.

In general, what do experts say is the best thing these new millionaires can do do to deal with all the weirdness that's about to come their way? Absolutely nothing.

Work with professionals to address the urgent legal, tax and financial matters, of course, but don't peacock, don't buy stuff, don't move, don't quit, don't believe for a moment that you are suddenly super hot based on all the new attention you're getting from the opposite sex. It's all just noise.

Bradley suggests taking a break from any decisions that don't need to be made. "Even if it's as simple as saying, 'This is big. It's a little overwhelming right now, a little more than I expected, and I'm going to take my time.' Just buy some space."

Fortunately, $10 million can buy a lot of space.

#2737. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2736. Budget carrier Norse Atlantic falls 78% after warning its finances are ‘critical’ amid soaring fuel costs

Norse Atlantic shares plummeted Wednesday after it revealed the company is in a "critical financial situation" as soaring fuel costs amid the Iran war strain budget carriers during the winter season.

The Norwegian low-cost carrier said its situation is dependent on securing financing for its short-term liquidity needs.

The company has had discussions about a potential strategic takeover as well as other options including ACMI contracts, which refer to short-term capacity leasing.

"Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution," it added.

The start of the U.S.-Iran war on Feb. 28 sent jet fuel prices soaring, putting pressure on airlines around the world. Prices are now up nearly 72% to $155 per barrel year-on-year as of the week ending Nov. 20, according to the International Air Transport Association's Jet Fuel Price Monitor.

Norse, which offers cheap long-haul flights between Europe, North America, Africa, and Asia, said in October that it was forced to fly with reduced capacity that month, due to "prolonged high fuel prices."

Norse Atlantic's CEO Eivind Roald told CNBC in May that he was not "overly concerned" about access to fuel and said the airline didn't have insight that the crisis would have an immediate impact.

"Fuel price rose by more than 100% and the beginning of March we had already sold most of our seats for March so it was difficult to overcompensate with higher prices for those few seats left," Roald said.

The airline had cancelled all flights to and from Los Angeles at the time due to the cost of jet fuel, impacting over 150,000 passengers. Roald also said Norse cancelled more than 700 flights in total, which impacted more than 240,000 passengers.

The company said in August that geopolitical disruptions and higher jet fuel costs hit profitability in the first half of the year. Higher fuel costs, lower aircraft use, and operational disruptions led to an $8.4 million second-quarter loss, measured before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization, and rent.

EasyJet, another low-cost airline impacted by high fuel costs, reported Wednesday that profit before tax slumped 89% to £71 million ($92.7 million) for the year ending in September 2026. Revenue growth was unable to offset the impact of an 11% increase in fuel costs due to the Middle East conflict, the company said.

Earlier this year, Ryanair's CEO Michael O'Leary told CNBC that other European carriers would struggle if jet fuel prices continued to soar. "I think there will be failures."

"If it continues at $150 a barrel into July, August, September, then you'll see European airlines fail and that, in the medium term, would probably be good for Ryanair's business."

Meanwhile, Ryanair's chief financial officer Neil Sorahan told CNBC in May: "I think we will see some of the weaker carriers who were already struggling before the war possibly go to the wall in the winter."

Several smaller European airlines have stopped flying this winter. Slovakia's AirExplore ceased operations, Ireland's Fly4 entered provisional liquidation, and Spain's AlbaStar suspended flights while seeking creditor protection.

Spain's Plus Ultra has also suspended all flights while it restructures, though it has not confirmed a permanent closure.

#2734. Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington

President Donald Trump wanted Jensen Huang back at the helm of Nvidia. Now that the chip mogul is reinstated, Trump is cheering alone in Washington.

Trump celebrated and claimed credit after Huang was reinstated by the Nvidia board on Monday, a stunning return to power for the embattled CEO. In a nearly hourlong phone call with CNBC, the president went as far as saying he "made the deal" to bring Huang back.

But Trump's jubilation stands in stark contrast to the reaction from even his staunchest allies on Capitol Hill, who recoiled after the reinstatement and vowed to continue their investigations into Huang — whose relationship with a potential Chinese intelligence asset they fear may have jeopardized U.S. national security.

"The risk remains that there could be information that a Chinese spy knows about a key individual in the supply chain, and that's not worth the risk," Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang for crying out loud ... just to make sure that he doesn't do something that's going to risk the United States."

Trump's rare isolation from his party over Huang comes after the GOP was throttled in the midterm elections, as Democrats rode a blue tsunami to capture the Senate and the largest House majority this century. And it suggests Republicans, who have spent a decade in lockstep with the president, may have found an issue on which they can't bring themselves to take Trump's side.

"I can accept what the president has done," Cramer said. "But we have to put guardrails around to protect the United States of America."

Many midterm voters identified Silicon Valley's most visible outputs, artificial intelligence and data centers, as top concerns motivating them to cast ballots for Democrats. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey in October found 63% of registered voters oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% support one.

By timing his extraordinary intervention in Nvidia so soon after the GOP's historic losses, Trump could spark a national debate about corporate governance and responsibility, former Under Secretary of State Richard Stengel said.

"With the repudiation of Trumpism in the midterms and voter revulsion with corruption, I think there will be a turn back to a more value-based duty of care for boards of directors and away from the current maximization of shareholder value," Stengel told CNBC in an email.

"Directors are citizens first, shareholders second. The idea that you put profit above national security should disgust shareholders, not please them," Stengel, who worked in the Obama administration, wrote.

Bipartisan lawmakers are now racing to pass a series of export control bills before the year ends, a call that has only grown louder since Huang was reinstated.

There's "not just frustration or political worry, but actual, substantive national security concern here from Democrats and Republicans," Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told CNBC.

"This has historically been a bipartisan issue," McGuire said. "Democrats and Republicans generally pretty much agree that we shouldn't be sending our most advanced chips to China."

"If it happened in massive quantities, people want to know why, how, and they want to make sure that it doesn't happen again," he said. "And putting your thumb on the scale in this clear of a way seems like it could undercut those efforts."

The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the political dynamics of Trump's involvement in reinstating Huang.

Republicans will have the first crack at investigating Huang next week before ceding power to Democrats in January. Democrats have vowed their own investigations into the Nvidia CEO and his ties to the president and his Cabinet. The Democrats who will lead those investigations are now hopeful that Republicans will join them.

"I've been seeing a lot of Republicans outraged and scandalized by what has just happened," House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., said Tuesday on "Squawk Box," when asked if Republicans may support a bipartisan investigation of Nvidia.

"When else in American history can you think of a time when a president of the United States called up a corporate board of directors meeting and then essentially dictated to them who was going to be their new CEO right after they had fired the guy?"

Trump throughout his second term has stated repeatedly that achieving AI dominance is required for the U.S. to maintain global superiority. His administration has championed the rapid growth of the country's tech giants and forged close ties with its leaders, especially Huang, while removing constraints on the industry and opposing some new regulatory efforts.

At the same time, Trump has defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick against accusations of slow-walking export controls on China, the fiercest competitor in the AI race. And while Trump recently discussed AI during an in-person meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, he appeared to deliver few demands and achieved few assurances about Beijing's efforts to acquire U.S. chips.

"To say we can't do AI safety because of China, and then also be actively loosening the controls on China, makes no sense," McGuire said.

Some of Trump's fiercest allies have raised similar qualms.

"Reinstating Jensen Huang is going to blow back on our national security," MAGA activist Laura Loomer wrote in an X post Monday. "Eventually there has to be accountability for jeopardizing US national security. China didn't just get access to Nvidia chips by accident."

Newt Gingrich, the influential former Republican speaker of the House, in an X post after Huang's reinstatement, wrote, "Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy."

Their criticisms sharply contrast with the praise coming from Silicon Valley and some of the Trump-friendly voices within it, such as Elon Musk, who wrote Monday, "The mistake has been corrected."

But that's a shrinking political constituency, McGuire said.

"The tech-right perspective is very out of touch with where most of the Republican Party is on these issues, to say nothing of the Democratic Party," he said.

"Those positions are just not going to be sustainable for much longer," he added. "I think they're already becoming unsustainable."

Hayes said he would like to see bitcoin rebound from around $55,000 even as the Nasdaq continues to fall. That divergence, he said, would suggest markets were shifting from a broad sell-off toward pricing in a "reflation" scenario, with the Federal Reserve eventually providing more liquidity.

Neither bitcoin nor gold has yet decoupled from the Nasdaq, with Hayes describing the current market moves as a "correlation-led liquidation."

"Stuff goes down, you sell crypto first because it's easy, and then you sell everything else," he said.

Hayes said a bitcoin rally could push up funding rates and futures-basis returns, increasing the income Ethena earns from its hedged crypto positions. That could make USDe, Ethena's synthetic dollar, more attractive and expand its circulation, he said, adding that he expects the ENA token to rise materially.

"Those are the two things that I'm keeping an eye on, and when I'm ready to pull the trigger on buying risk again, those will be the things we buy a lot of," Hayes said.

#2730. Wealthy investors seek tax savings from municipal bonds as yields remain elevated

The business of tax-loss harvesting is booming with wealthy investors pouring billions of dollars into products like tax-aware long-short strategies. As 10-year Treasury yields have climbed to levels not seen since 2007, tax-savvy clients are also turning to municipal bonds to keep more of what they earn.

"High-net-worth investors, because of all the noise in direct indexing and tax-aware long-short strategies, have begun to expect tax management from all of their investments, including their fixed income," said Gavin Romm, senior vice president and head of separately managed accounts at AllianceBernstein.

While tax-loss harvesting can be done with other types of fixed income, high-income investors typically gravitate to municipal bonds for their tax-exempt income. Separately managed accounts, known as SMAs, held about $1.6 trillion in municipal bonds at the end of 2025, a 44% jump since 2017, per JPMorgan's estimate.

For top-bracket investors, municipal bonds can offer a twofold benefit: tax-equivalent yields that approach long-run stock-market returns, and losses that may offset gains elsewhere in a portfolio, according to Ran Leshem, BlackRock's head of SMA solutions. BlackRock, which manages $42 billion in muni SMAs, estimates that assets across muni SMAs have grown by 10% industry-wide over the past three years.

"You can get a tax-equivalent yield of over 7% that is becoming quite compelling for a lot of clients," said Leshem. "We are seeing yields that haven't been around for quite a few years, so it's a good opportunity for clients to lock in yields at these higher rates."

Rising yields earlier this fall pushed bond prices down, leaving some investors with paper losses, Leshem said. However, tax-loss harvesting can be harder with bonds than with stock, particularly municipal bonds, he noted. The municipal bond market is highly fragmented with more than 50,000 issuers, and it costs more and takes longer to transact, he said.

"There might not always be liquidity or someone willing to buy it for a fair price," Leshem said.

That said, bonds can offer a distinct tax advantage from equities, according to Romm.

By selling a stock at a loss, an investor can reduce the current tax bill by offsetting gains elsewhere. In exchange, the investor faces a potentially larger taxable gain if they later sell the replacement stock.

However, if an investor sells a bond at a loss and buys a replacement bond for more than its par value (or face value) the replacement bond's tax basis is generally adjusted down over time as it approaches maturity, Romm said. If the investor holds it to maturity, the amount repaid may match that adjusted basis, leaving no capital gain or loss on the replacement bond, he added.

"Tax-loss harvesting with equities, by definition, is tax deferral," he said. "With bonds, when done thoughtfully, it is actually tax avoidance."

That said, investors must be careful not to violate the IRS wash-sale rule by buying a "substantially identical asset" within 30 days before or after the sale.

That tax benefit gives fixed income another job beyond providing income and stability, Romm said.

"These aren't really positioned as get-rich strategies. They're more of stay-rich strategies," he said.

The Inside Wealth newsletter by Robert Frank is your weekly guide to high-net-worth investors and the industries that serve them.
