#2698. SpaceX wins FCC approval to deploy 1 million orbital data center satellites

The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday.

Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI.

Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

The FCC, in its authorization filing, noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC (Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)."

In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan."

The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims."

The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr, who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone.

Amazon declined to comment on the FCC's approval.

Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher, which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October.

In March, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January.

Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday.

"Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense."

SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."

Vance spoke two days after President Donald Trump told CNBC in an interview that an investigation had been done.

Trump was asked what Blanche had told him about potential criminal liability for Huang and the question of whether Nvidia chips had ended up in China in violation of U.S. export laws.

"They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said Monday.

Reuters reported Wednesday that the Department of Justice did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before Trump pushed for his reinstatement as CEO.

Blanche had concluded there was no evidence Huang had broken any laws based on investigations into Nvidia clients Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed, according to the report.

The DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Reuters report. And the White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Vance saying Huang was under no investigation when Trump had said there was one. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about Vance's remarks.

Blanche on Tuesday dodged questions about whether there had been an investigation.

"What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him," Blanche said after being asked whether the DOJ had investigated Huang and, if so, what were the results of the probe.

Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, after the chipmaker's board of directors said it had received "input from senior levels of the United States government" that Huang was not a national security risk. Trump took credit for Huang's reinstatement in the interview with CNBC shortly after Nvidia's announcement.

Huang resigned following The New York Times reporting multiple affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing and who was an executive for the Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed.

The reporting added fuel to allegations that Nvidia should have known its artificial intelligence chips were being diverted to China and being used by Chinese companies, violating U.S. export laws.

"The product they create is a very important part of us staying ahead of the SI arms race with China. We really do care about ensuring those chips do not fall into the wrong hands," Vance said, using the Trump administration's preferred acronym for AI, which the president calls "super intelligence."

"We actually see this is an opportunity for Nvidia to focus on complying with American export controls, and we think Jensen Huang is going to take that very seriously," Vance continued.

"We received the assurances that he was not under any significant — he was under no investigation — and the accusations against him were based on anonymous reporting, not on actual evidence," Vance said.

On Tuesday, Trump left the door open to pardon Huang in an interview with the New York Post, but Vance said on Wednesday that the CEO doesn't need one.

"I don't think he needs a pardon at all," Vance said. "I haven't seen any evidence again that he committed a crime. And if there is evidence that he committed a crime, then that's up to relevant authorities to actually bring a prosecution against him."

Huang is scheduled to appear for a closed-door interview with House committees about his dealings with Megaspeed on Tuesday. At the same time, Nvidia will hold its annual conference where it showcases new technology in Washington.

— Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

Before Dybantsa committed to BYU, became a collegiate superstar, and went No. 1 in the 2026 NBA Draft, he attended Tatum's basketball camp. Back then, he was a youth prospect just starting to build buzz at Saint Sebastian's School in Needham, Mass., before transferring to Prolific Prep in Napa, Calif., and once more to Utah Prep Academy in Hurricane, Utah.

Tatum took the time to get to know Dybantsa and share some advice. So when the two crossed paths again, this time as fellow professionals, Dybantsa was struck by the moment. He did, however, admit it could be even bigger when they meet for the rematch on Dec. 14 at TD Garden.

"I think it'll be more surreal when I play over there, but today was definitely a cool moment," Dybantsa said.

Nearly a year later, Dybantsa put on a show to win over Washington's crowd, finishing with 20 points, 11 rebounds and a career-high seven assists against the No. 2 seed Celtics.

Dybantsa is averaging 20 points, 9.2 rebounds and 4.8 assists on 45.6 percent shooting over his last five games. He shot 7-for-18 on Tuesday night and knocked down a pair of threes, which, to Tatum, is just a sneak peek of what's to come in the near future from Dybantsa.

Tatum put on a show himself, eager to get Boston back in the win column amid its four-game losing streak.

The second game of the 2026 chess world championship between defending champion Gukesh Dommaraju and challenger Javokhir Sindarov also ended in a draw on Wednesday.

Each win is worth one point, while a draw is worth half a point. Players are not allowed to agree to a draw before Black's 40th move. A draw claim before then is only permitted if a threefold repetition or stalemate had occurred.

#2693. Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.

The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.

Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.

Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.

But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.

Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.

"You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.

Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.

"The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3."

While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.

Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.

"There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets.

Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.

Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.

A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.

"If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."

For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.

Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.

Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.

One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#2691. 2027 Browns mock draft: Selecting a potential turkey at quarterback

The Cleveland Browns have surprisingly played themselves into the AFC playoff race, sitting one game behind the Cincinnati Bengals for first in the AFC North.

Playing meaningful games rather than focusing on draft position is a refreshing change of pace for the franchise. But it does not erase the reality that the Browns will be rebuilding the quarterback room in 2027.

Just what that remodeling will look like is still in the "to be determined" file, as the Browns could:

Run it back with the current group (not at all likely).

Decide it is time to unleash Shedeur Sanders as the starter on an unsuspecting NFL (literally not happening).

Some mix of the always popular veteran "bridge quarterback" to pair with a rookie selected in the 2027 NFL Draft. (Quite possible, even if that bridge is current starter Deshaun Watson, which no one would have seen coming a few months ago).

That final bullet point brings us to a mock draft from Nate Tice at Yahoo Sports, which, unfortunately, has the Browns embracing the Thanksgiving spirit by selecting a potential turkey at the quarterback position.

Tice projects the Browns to be selecting at No. 17 (with the selection they received from the Los Angeles Rams as part of the Myles Garrett trade) and No. 20 (with their own pick).

With that first selection, Tice embraces the "Browns is the Browns" mantra by selecting South Carolina quarterback LaNorris Sellers:

The Browns throw another dart at the quarterback position. And boy, what a chance of hitting the bull's-eye this would be. Sellers is young (important to the Browns process) and has some of the loudest tools you'll ever see at the position. His play has felt calmer and more decisive over the past month, but he will need more time, especially in a more conducive situation than the one he's been in the past few years. Landing in Cleveland with the Browns' exciting young group of pass catchers isn't the worst place to settle, especially with head coach Todd Monken, who has gotten the most out of his quarterbacks at multiple stops.

Sellers is one of the most divisive college quarterbacks, which is saying a lot given the expected draft class. While athletic, he has only completed 63.1 percent of his career passes, while most top quarterbacks surpass 70 percent. He tosses interceptions (23), which are not really balanced out by just 50 touchdown passes.

Sellers is a quarterback who will have big games, like his four-touchdown performance this season against Florida – but offset that with clunkers, like completing 56 percent of his passes against Tennessee or throwing for just 87 yards against Georgia.

The Browns have searched so long for a quarterback, and made a mess of it far too often, that it is hard to see how selecting a player who is going to need a year (or likely more) to develop, with no guarantee of success.

Three picks later, Tice adds some depth to the defense with the selection of Notre Dame defensive end Boubacar Traore:

I peeked at another offensive lineman here, despite this year's Spencer Fano selection, and hit on the Austin Barber pick. Funnily enough, I have compared Traore to Jared Verse (but might be leaning more toward a DeMarcus Lawrence comparison). Either way, those are two strong defenders who can push the pocket, and that's exactly what Traore brings to the table. He would be another strong edge defender to add to the Browns' front.

The Browns can always use help on defense, and in 32 career games, Traore has 88 tackles, 15.5 sacks, and 26.5 tackles for loss. His draft stock has been rising this season, and if the Irish make a run through the college football playoffs, Traore will have plenty of opportunities to showcase his talent against tougher competition than the likes of Rice, Navy, and Purdue.

So there you have it. The Browns "throw another dart" at the quarterback position and add some help for the defensive line with a player who might be Jared Verse 2.0.

#2687. How to prevent Browns' slow starts on defense? It's all about a spark

BEREA ― It's from a simple spark that a giant inferno starts.

The Browns defense believes it's as simple as a spark for them to turn into one of the better defenses in the league. It's just about finding that consistent spark to light the fire.

"I think we had somebody on defense say it perfectly," defensive end Jared Verse said Nov. 25. "Once somebody makes a play, everyone's locked in. But until then, we just got to get out there and make a play as fast as possible instead of waiting for somebody else."

Who the unknown defender was to theorize that may have a point. Although, it may not be a point entirely shared by everyone on the defense.

"Yeah, I think there could be an aspect of that," linebacker Carson Schwesinger said. "I think it's just a matter of all of us being ready a little bit quicker, not taking a drive or two to get going. I think some of it's that, some of it is other things, but I think just being ready to start from play one and take the style of defense that we know we play and do it for all 60 minutes."

The Browns defense is coming out of the bye ranked No. 16 in total yards allowed (327.4), No. 23 in rushing yards allowed (126.3) and No. 6 in passing yards allowed (201.1). Part of the reasons why those rankings sit where they do rest in the way they have struggled to come out of the gates strong in almost every game.

For all of the talk about offensive issues from the start, the defense has dealt with a similar problem. It's been something that was a topic of conversation before the break, and it remained one coming back as the Browns turn their attention to their "Sunday Night Football" meeting with the Las Vegas Raiders.

"Yeah, I think definitely starting fast," cornerback Denzel Ward said, "just trying to clean up those things and yeah, just being who we are. Getting back to who we are, applying pressure on the quarterback and playing coverage in the back end."

Opponents have scored on their first possession in all but two games this season, and one of those was a missed field goal by the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 8. The Browns have been down 14-0 to the Jacksonville Jaguars, 10-0 to the Baltimore Ravens, 14-0 to the Tennessee Titans and 10-0 to the Houston Texans in the first quarter.

The thing is, the Browns rallied to win three of those four games. They understand that getting off to better starts is part of the equation to fix a lot of the issues holding them back.

"Oh, to be elite, you got to stop the run," Schwesinger said. "I think specifically for us, we got to be able to go out there and start fast and then you just limit explosives in the pass game. You're able to do those three things and then also create turnovers. We always say the ball's oxygen and you do that and you'll be an elite defense."

The Browns have had their share of big plays on defense, although those numbers aren't quite as high as they would necessarily like. They have 27 sacks, which is tied for 11th, while they've created 13 takeaways, which is tied for 14th.

The bigger issue goes back to what Schwesinger said about the theory. It's about playing each of the 60 minutes the same.

"We all like the idea of big plays for sure, but it really comes down to, I've said this before, and we believe it in our hearts," defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg said, "whether it's the first play, the last play, the first drive, the fifth drive, the 10th drive, there's no defining moments of a game because every play matters. And it's easy to look at things and say, 'Oh, we didn't start fast. We didn't finish well. We're good at this. We were bad at this.'

"But the truth is a consistent execution is what we're all looking for. Finding that winning edge, shrinking that margin where it's not Browns hurting Browns, where it's Browns helping Browns, which goes to your point about making a big play, but it's constantly searching to be consistent. I mean, that's what this league is and the most consistent teams win.

#2683. Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’

Cathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds.

Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm.

"We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business.

Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday.

"We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here."

The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic.

In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF, Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX, representing more than 21% of the fund together.

Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses.

The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year.

Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble.

"Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

#2675. Putting Phoenix’s four-game winning streak into perspective

The Phoenix Suns have fought and clawed their way back above .500, and as they sit at 9-7 preparing to face the Houston Rockets in NBA Cup play tonight, one common question is being asked: Are they legit, or are they simply beating up on bad teams?

This is one of those situations where I feel like multiple things can be true at once. Yes, the Suns have gotten right during a valley in their competition's quality. And I would certainly take these results over dropping a game or two against subpar competition, something we've become all too familiar with in recent years. Many would find themselves stewing had they dropped a game to Utah or were defeated by the Kings.

How legit are they? Time will ultimately tell. I look at it through this lens: Where did you predict the Suns would finish the season? The majority of Bright Side readers had them falling somewhere in the 44 to 47 win range. At 9-7? They're on pace for 46 wins.

So, despite the interesting journey to get to this point, the Suns are kind of exactly who we thought they were. They're a team that most certainly has flaws, possesses the ability to be competitive, and can win games. They reside somewhere between the NBA's elite teams and the basement dwellers.

What we've witnessed thus far is a reminder that the journey to whatever the final record may be isn't linear. It's one defined by peaks and valleys, opportunities presented by the schedule, and those unfortunate back-to-backs against quality competition where it feels like you're being set up to lose. How many times did we play Oklahoma City or San Antonio last season on the second night of a back-to-back, am I right?

Tonight's game against Houston will be an interesting one, considering the Rockets enter at 13-5 and possess one of the best offenses in the league. And should the Suns lose? Many will sprint to their keyboards, overreact to the result, and begin questioning the current state of the Phoenix Suns. I'd advise against that. Remember that this journey is a long and winding road, and for a team that resides somewhere in the middle, those results are to be expected.

The Suns don't need to prove they're a championship contender tonight. They need to keep building, keep finding ways to win, and continue showing that the team we thought could compete is, in fact, capable of competing. A loss to Houston wouldn't erase the progress they've made. A win would certainly add another layer of intrigue to the conversation.

But let's be honest. If they beat the Rockets, I'm not interested in hearing about strength of schedule anymore. Clear the parade route. We're winning a championship.

#2673. Top Wall Street analysts favor these 3 dividend stocks for strong returns

Investors often favor dividend stocks for their regular income and the promise of potential share price appreciation. But selecting the right dividend stocks from a huge pool of companies can be difficult.

Top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend-paying stocks, as their recommendations are backed by thorough analysis of a company's financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Devon Energy (DVN), an independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company, reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. The company announced a quarterly dividend of 32 cents per share for the fourth quarter, payable December 30. Based on the fixed dividends paid over the trailing 12 months, DVN yields 2.85%.

After hosting a virtual investor meeting with management, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Devon, with a price target of $59. Mehta said that he is now more confident in management's outlook for delivering strong near-term capital returns as well as efforts to drive operational efficiencies and productivity gains.

Devon sees an opportunity to increase share repurchases, driven by solid free cash flow (FCF), contributions from the Eagle Ford divestiture and continued improvement in the balance sheet, Mehta said. Devon expects share buybacks worth more than $1 billion in Q4 2026, up from $414 million in the third quarter, backed by a strong pricing backdrop and improved capital efficiency.

Mehta, a 5-star analyst, said Devon expects about $6.3 billion of excess FCF in 2027, including about $3.5 billion of net proceeds from the Eagle Ford sale. That would enable the company to accelerate buybacks while progressing toward its goal of reducing gross debt to about $9 billion by early 2027. Mehta noted that under DVN's framework to return up to 70% of annual FCF, management favors share buybacks as it believes the stock is discounted compared to large-cap peers.

"Management expects continued capital efficiency gains from merger synergies, extended laterals, surfactant adoption and development of the newly acquired federal acreage," Mehta said.

Mehta ranks No. 876 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 8.1%. See Devon Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Energy Transfer (ET), is a limited partnership that operates about 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated energy infrastructure. The company recently announced third-quarter results showing net income per common unit growing about 18% year-over-year, to 33 cents. ET's cash distribution for Q3 2026 was 34.25 cents per common unit, up more than 3% year-over-year. At an annualized distribution of $1.37 per share, Energy Transfer yields more than 7%.

TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Energy Transfer with a price target of $25. The company delivered better-than-expected Q3 results and announced the 1.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcf/d) South Mississippi Pipeline, a 215-mile, 36-inch natural gas line linking the Perryville Hub to the Florida Gas Transmission (FGT) network, Gabelman said. The project is supported by 20-year firm transportation agreements and is expected to enter service in 2030. ET expects to ultimately own 51% of the $1.6 billion project.

The 5-star analyst said that Energy Transfer lowered its 2026 capital spending outlook to $5.5 billion (midpoint of the guidance range) from $5.75 billion due to project timing. Energy Transfer expects capex to rise to $7 billion in 2027, while Gabelman projects $5 billion in both 2028 and 2029, based on disclosed projects.

Gabelman also highlighted management's commentary about optimization initiatives contributing an incremental $800 million to 2026 earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, a larger benefit than in recent years. "A return to less commodity volatility should the [Middle East] war end could bring some relative downside, though this is offset by continued strong growth prospects," he said.

Gabelman ranks No. 397 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.4%. See Energy Transfer KPIs on TipRanks.

Oil and gas exploration and production company ConocoPhillips (COP) delivered better-than-expected Q3 performance. The company announced an 11% hike in its quarterly dividend to 93 cents per share, effective with the Q4 dividend payable on December 1. Based on the dividends paid over the trailing 12 months, COP yields about 2.6%.

Following the Q3 results, Wells Fargo analyst Sam Margolin repeated a buy rating on ConocoPhillips, citing strong potential for further dividend increases. Margolin also trimmed his price target to $185 from $189 to reflect timing effects and the WAHA forward curve, though he said that COP could still re-rate as its natural portfolio lifecycle provides stronger protection against inflationary pressures than peers. The Waha forward curve tracks future natural gas prices based on the West Texas Waha hub.

Margolin, another 5-star analyst, highlighted that ConocoPhillips' Q3 2026 adjusted earnings per share of $3.27 was well above Wells Fargo and the Street's estimates of $3.04 and $3.05, respectively. Earnings were driven by solid price realizations, partially offset by higher depletion, depreciation and amortization and purchased commodities.

Margolin also noted COP's dividend increase and said the accelerated buyback enabled by current commodity prices could further support long-term dividend growth. He sees the possibility of ConocoPhillips' dividend growth rate exceeding its current 6% cost of equity into the end of the decade. Margolin expects COP to sustain an 8% dividend compound annual growth rate through 2029 while repurchasing $6.4 billion of stock annually, and reducing net debt-to-capital to less than 9% by the end of 2028 based on the assumption of an average Brent crude oil price of $75 a barrel.

#2671. The biggest money-making energy trade looks over. What to buy instead

Is one of the greatest money-making trades of the last few years coming to an end?

No, I'm not talking about Nvidia or any of the data center- or AI-related power companies (although they have been crushed lately too… more on that on CNBC TV. Tune in!).

I'm talking about whether the epic boom in refinery-related stocks is unwinding. Over the last year, the jump in some of these companies has been nothing short of remarkable.

That jump is largely due to massive increases in margins, earnings, and cash flow. Those have occurred because of a big jump in what is called a crack spread. That is the difference between the price of oil and the finished price of refined products such as diesel and jet fuel. For most of this year, spreads have been soaring as disruptions and attacks on facilities and shipping in the Arabian Gulf, Hormuz, and deep inside Russia have played havoc with the market. In the last week or so, however, something big has changed: many of those spreads have started to tighten.

This seismic drop in spreads is causing a selloff in the aforementioned refinery companies.

If spreads continue to fall, these stocks may well keep selling off from recent highs. The upshot for investors may be that, as the shares come down, analysts see more upside. The median price target for Phillips 66 (PSX) now indicates a 20% gain from here, while smaller-cap Par Pacific (PARR) is double that.

Here are a few other key points to focus on heading into the Thanksgiving-shortened week.

I like to keep politics as much at arm's length as possible — we all know that energy and politics (sadly) often go hand in hand. Energy policies coming from Washington, D.C., can drive — or destroy — investment dollars. With all the big shifts in the White House over the last 10 years (four years of Trump, four years of Biden, and now 2 years into Trump #2), energy policies can blow through Washington faster than a summer squall hits a wind turbine. But because federal policies can mean so much for specific companies, sectors, and investments, it's important to follow the news flow.

That said, I'd like to take a moment to introduce you to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA (and pronounced like the state in Mexico). Like much legislation, BAAJA is an obscure but important bill working its way through the American Congress. BAAJA does a lot of things, but what Power Insider readers care about is its focus on energy permitting reform. In a nutshell, BAAJA would help speed up the building of new electricity infrastructure. Again, that's an overly simplistic view of a big bill, but it needs to be on your radar. The utility trade group Edison Electric Institute came out in favor of the legislation this month after the industry received some 11th-hour changes. See more about it in our recent interview with EEI President Drew Maloney here.

The bill passed the U.S. Senate in a vote late Thursday night. Now it moves to the House. Support for its final passage is also coming from the big LNG trade group, whose executive director said he "applauds the Senate for its bipartisan effort to pass meaningful, bipartisan, and durable permitting reforms aimed at delivering greater predictability, consistency, and certainty in the permitting, production, and export process for U.S. LNG. This legislation moves us closer to untangling red tape and eliminating overlapping agency reviews that can keep U.S. energy projects delayed for years."

The Natural Gas Supply Association also chimed in, saying it urges Congress to see the bill as "a resource-agnostic and balanced reform agenda for boosting American energy security. It keeps strong environmental reviews in place, but it draws a firm line against the endless procedural delays that tie critical energy projects in knots for a decade."

In my view, passing BAAJA is an important test of Congress's appetite for helping the energy and electrical power industry, lowering costs, and speeding time to market. The old adage was correct: time is money. Literally. If BAAJA moves on through the House, we could see an upside move in some utility stocks and any company related to energy infrastructure.

Speaking of politics, the news is getting lost in the massive Anthropic (ANT) IPO, but the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) — whose importance I wrote about in the last edition — just decided to resume permitting for data centers. The Texas Tribune did a nice write-up on it, and you can read it here.

It's tough to say, but it's true. The two are inextricably linked by policies created at both the federal and state levels. As I wrote in the last edition, some federally elected officials may have less impact on state-level issues — like the data center buildout — but they certainly have power over national laws. While many of you are enthralled, disgusted, or confused by sordid tales of Nvidia and Jensen-gate, keep one eye open on what happens in Washington, D.C.

Have a great week, and have a wonderful Thanksgiving, everyone.

Perhaps the big investor story — which is, like most things lately, related to Jensen-gate and Nvidia—is the sizable selloff in many AI, neocloud, and data center power-related stocks.

Painful for current shareholders, but big drops can also bring big opportunities. Wall Street believes that's the case, at least right now. Look at some of the potential upside based on the stocks' prices versus their price targets.

We spoke with the CEO of Applied Digital (APLD) about all of this on CNBC last week, and you can watch it here. He highlighted how the market may be getting these stock stories wrong because, at least with his company, he has long-term contracts with solid-credit companies. In that way, Applied Digital is more like a landlord than a "pure-play" AI company.

My take → While I'm not going to recommend a specific stock, I would add that it is critical for investors to understand the differences between these companies. While they may have some things in common, they are also different, with different business models, customers, leases, and sources of revenue.

Speaking of recommendations… here are two ideas for you:

A recent decline presents a nice opportunity in SOLV Energy (MWH). UBS analyst Jon Windham upgrades SOLV to buy from neutral, believing the market is "underappreciating several key tailwinds for SOLV given uncertainty around data center demand and higher interest rates." UBS highlights how the stock has fallen lately despite making two deals and beating and raising recent guidance. UBS says now is an "attractive entry point" for SOLV. (Side note: MWH is a great stock ticker.)

While markets overall fall, BMO remains bullish on Bloom Energy (BE). After speaking with the company, the analyst is upgrading Bloom to outperform, saying he remains "increasingly confident of BE's commercial traction" and that he still has conviction even with the recent drop in shares. While analyst Ameet Thakkar did cut his target to $230 from $260, that's still 50% upside from the current price. Bloom shares have tumbled 45% since October 1.

I was recently asked for my opinion on the price of oil. Here's my take. The market clearly wants to push oil contract prices lower and has for a few months. But, as I've said and reported for a while, don't confuse the futures (paper) price with the actual price. Yes, shipping rates and insurance rates have come down from recent highs — and there is a good amount of oil now flowing through Hormuz — but the cost of a physical barrel of crude is still well above the futures contract. If we get real, longer-lasting peace around Iran, oil prices will fall. There is plenty of oil in the world. That said, if bombs and missiles start firing again, oil prices will firm. I know that's a non-answer answer, but the oil market is truly headline-driven right now. My late good friend Boone Pickens (later in life, he didn't like being called by the "T" in his first name) used to avoid giving a set price target and instead give a directional quote, so I'll do the same: the odds of oil being lower in two months than it is today are 75%.

Last week, I had a one-on-one with Vimal Kapur, chair and CEO of Honeywell International (HON), at an RBC conference in New York City. While the conversation wasn't filmed, I can tell you that Kapur offered investors reassurance that his order book is doing very, very well. This is important because Honeywell is huge in the things that make other things work. Its sensors go into a ton of energy facilities, from refineries to LNG facilities. Honeywell is a leading indicator of spending and buildouts, so if it keeps getting orders, it's a good sign for macro energy.

Bottom line: Watch Honeywell stock as a potential "tell."

This week's Inside Line interview takes a different approach. We hit our friend Craig Johnson up for actionable insights into energy and stocks. Craig is managing director and chief market technician at Piper Sandler. He recently appeared on Power Lunch to talk about markets and stocks. He mentioned being bullish on energy, so we wanted to dig in just a little bit more.

This week, we had the pleasure of chatting with Balaji Krishnamurthy, president of Chevron Australia. We spoke at length about natural gas, the impact of disruptions, and long-term demand from Chevron customers in the Asia-Pacific region.

This is a bit of a local RBI for the New York City area, but one I felt was important to highlight. New York's electric grid operator just came out with a massive warning for everyone in our region: in just a couple of years, there may not be enough electricity supply to power our needs. A new report shows a deficit in seven years, with a nearly 2 GW power hole in a decade. That's a number of big power plants' worth of energy. Get your solar panels on and buy that backup generator! I'll call this one random, but scary.

#2670. NBA announces $11 billion investment to build European arenas for new league

The NBA has unveiled a $11 billion funding initiative aimed at developing and renovating basketball arenas across Europe. This investment is designed to support the launch of the new NBA and FIBA-created European League that could see its inaugural tip-off as soon as next fall.

On Wednesday, Nov. 25, the NBA announced a detailed strategic partnership with a coalition of leading global investment firms, including Apollo Sports Capital, Ares Management, Arctos, Blackstone, HPS Investment Partners, J.P. Morgan and others. These firms will spearhead the funding initiative, collaborating closely with participating clubs, team owners, local developers and a range of service providers. Together, they aim to construct and upgrade world-class basketball arenas.

According to the NBA, the initiative will "provide prospective clubs and ownership groups with access to sustainable capital and the NBA's expertise to develop modern arena facilities and, where appropriate, surrounding districts."

More: NBA power rankings: How far will slumping Thunder, Celtics fall?

The NBA and FIBA have also emphasized that this initiative represents a significant investment not only in the sport itself, but also in the economic vitality of host cities. New or renovated arenas are expected to drive local growth and create jobs.

"We've seen firsthand how state-of-the-art arenas and the related developments around them can transform basketball teams and their surrounding communities," NBA commissioner Adam Silver said in a statement. "As we prepare to launch a new league in Europe alongside FIBA, we see a significant opportunity to help clubs develop facilities which both build on the unique traditions that define European basketball while also elevating the fan experience and attracting many more live events."

While official host cities have yet to be announced, the NBA-FIBA project is reportedly considering several countries as prime candidates for the new league.

Potential host cities include London and Manchester (Britain), Paris and Lyon (France), Madrid and Barcelona (Spain), Rome and Milan (Italy), Munich and Berlin (Germany), Athens (Greece) and Istanbul (Turkey).

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: NBA announces $11 billion investment to build European arenas for new league

#2667. Nvidia surge: What investors should do with the stock and the AI trade now

Nvidia shares gapped higher at the open by more than 30%, on pace for its biggest one-day gain in 23 years on Monday, following the news just before the bell that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is going to be reinstated.

Investors and traders said that while this reflex rally may have more to run, cautiousness is warranted on Nvidia and the AI trade because of the overhang of investigations into the alleged Chinese espionage involving the company and others, as well as the possibility for data center moratoriums as Democrats take control of Congress and key governor posts in January.

"Am I as bullish on Nvidia now as I was on Friday? Of course not, you can't be," said Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, which counted Nvidia as its largest position as he bought on the dip over the last few weeks. "I'm trimming back."

"All the same issues that were here before Jensen resigned are still here," he added.

The day before Huang resigned on Nov. 12 as CEO, Nvidia closed at $173.73. It's intraday high on Monday was $171.50, up from its recent low around $125 as it was selling off in the wake controversies. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF closed at $506.96 the day before his resignation. It reached a high of $469.35 before losing steam as trading wore on Monday.

Mike Khouw, YieldMax strategist at Tidal Financial Group, told CNBC on Monday that there were "sighs of relief," "applause" and even "cheering" among investors at the news of Huang's potential reinstatement. But he also said there are still considerable risks facing the AI trade.

Jensen Huang was not the only problem at Nvidia, he said, and there are still many vulnerabilities in the overall AI trade, which should give investors pause. Credit-sensitive companies are still at risk of faltering, Khouw added.

The national security implications of the scandal that has rocked Nvidia and the global AI trade more broadly aren't going away any time soon even as the Trump administration assured the Nvidia board there were none. Investors on Wall Street are expressing strategic concerns about ways to play the tech space just as lawmakers in Washington are demanding answers.

Democrats are demanding answers on what exactly happened with Nvidia and the Chinese government.

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a Monday statement. "The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement."

House Ways and Means ranking member Richard Neal (D-Mass.) stressed the importance of Congressional oversight in determining the best course of action to move forward. The outcome of any Congressional investigations will likely be crucial for Nvidia's long-term viability as an investment opportunity, especially since the company does so much international business.

"This is an export control issue," Neal told CNBC on Monday. "Congress is not subservient to this president or any other president as it relates to trade and tariff policies. This is a trade related issue."

Many of the same Democrats will call for a slowdown in the data center buildout, a strong issue for the public partly responsible for their Blue Wave earlier this month.

"You're going to have to work your way through what these data center moratoriums all mean," said Niles. "Now I think the broader market keeps going but I am not as convinced on the move in the data-center centric names from here."

To be sure, many Wall Street analysts were rushing to upgrade Nvidia's stock on Monday after Huang's reinstatement. Most restored price targets well above $200 with one as high as $270. But many traders think the rebound may fail before getting back to those levels.

Famed short seller Michael Burry, who made a boatload betting against Nvidia with put options as it cratered, told his Substack audience that he thinks the rebound here could be "outsized," especially with low volume in the market overall because of the Thanksgiving holiday this week.

But he too sees the rally eventually losing steam.

"Jensen being back without much more information might even restore NVDA to the high 100s," Burry wrote. "I won't short it on this information I have today until it gets closer to or maybe hurdles $200."

#2663. CBF Academy Summit gathers experts to debate Brazilian football's future

On Wednesday (25), the Tivoli hotel in São Paulo hosted the third edition of the CBF Academy Summit, an event dedicated to discussing various aspects of the Brazilian football ecosystem. This year's central theme was "Debating the future of Brazilian football," with a program featuring 18 panels made up of CBF representatives, Brazilian club officials and football industry experts.

The event was opened by CBF vice-president Gustavo Dias Henrique and Brazil head coach Carlo Ancelotti, with the discussion moderated by the organization's communications director, Fabio Seixas. Dias highlighted the challenges facing the current CBF administration, which has been delivering unprecedented progress in Brazilian football.

"Some people bet that the new CBF would bring more of the same, but we are a highly qualified group that came here to change our football. Several new projects will be unveiled in 2027, when another major focus will be putting our national team back on top," said the vice-president.

CBF vice-president Gustavo Dias Henrique highlighted the progress being driven by the current CBF administrationCredits: Handout

The event's main hall drew a large audience for the panel "Planning for Brazil's Men's National Teams," which brought together the leadership of the Men's National Teams Department: alongside head coach Carlo Ancelotti were Rodrigo Caetano, general executive coordinator of the Men's National Teams; Cícero Souza, general manager of the Men's National Teams; Juan Santos, technical coordinator of the Brazilian national team; and Paulo Victor Gomes, head coach of Brazil's Under-20 team.

Ancelotti discussed Brazil's plans for 2027, focusing on making the most of the two FIFA international windows in March and June, which will feature crucial matches ahead of the season's major challenges: the Copa América and the qualifiers for the 2030 World Cup.

"The Copa América is the first objective. We are very confident because we have seen a lot of good things in our scouting. We have the tools to build a strong squad," he said.

Brazil head coach Carlo Ancelotti: "The Copa América is the first objective"Credits: Handout

Executive coordinator Rodrigo Caetano detailed the challenges facing the National Teams Department during Brazil's preparation cycle. With higher-quality opponents unavailable, the team used recent friendlies to fulfill another part of its plan: assessing players to refresh the squad.

"This year, European and African teams were unavailable because of continental competitions. So, to make the recent friendlies worthwhile from a sporting perspective, we adopted a policy of bringing in younger players, calling up a majority who play in Brazil, according to established criteria. But we are aware of the draw dates for European international competitions and are already looking at which national teams will be available in March and June for the warm-up friendlies before the qualifiers," he explained.

Juan Santos highlighted the processes introduced within the department to gather information on Brazilian players, supporting Carlo Ancelotti's squad selections. According to the technical coordinator, the current gap between friendlies, from November this year to March 2027, will be used to visit clubs and stay in touch with players being monitored by the coaching staff. The integration of Brazil's national teams across age groups, which has been strengthened under the current administration, was illustrated by the career of forward Rayan, who played for the Under-17s and Under-20s and reached the World Cup within three years.

This integration was reinforced by Under-20 head coach Paulo Victor, who highlighted this year's match planning for the age group, allowing thorough preparation for a return to winning titles in 2027, with the South American Championship in January and the World Cup in September.

Rodrigo Caetano during the panel "Planning for Brazil's Men's National Teams"Credits: Handout

The coordinated work spanning the Under-15s through to the senior team includes coaching methodologies applied across all teams while respecting the specific needs of each age group. According to Cícero, this philosophy was strengthened through FIFA TDS, a three-day immersion program that brought the coaching staffs of all age groups together at Granja Comary.

The program established five pillars that should define Brazilian football: joy, creativity, unity, a winning spirit and courage. "These pillars are supported by 33 behaviors that should be demonstrated on the pitch, such as dribbling, for example," Souza explained.

During the panel "The calendar and the future of broadcasting rights: challenges and prospects," CBF competitions director Julio Avellar discussed the factors that guided the development of Brazilian football's new calendar.

The new schedule reduced the number of matches for overburdened teams and increased fixtures for smaller clubs, creating opportunities for greater exposure and revenue. It also gave broadcast rights holders more predictable scheduling, while rewarding Brazilian fans with plenty of opportunities to watch their teams.

Julio Avellar: "Changes to the calendar have given broadcast rights holders greater predictability"Credits: Handout

According to Avellar, Brazilian football now has a calendar that "protects" Brazilian clubs. "We have midyear breaks for competitions such as the Club World Cup and the men's and women's World Cups. This enhances the value of assets such as the Copa do Brasil and the Brasileirão," he said.

The changes have made it possible to establish fixed broadcast slots, giving companies that purchase match broadcasting rights greater predictability. "Previously, up to 60% of the published fixture schedule would change. Today, that figure is below 10%," he noted.

During the panel "Refereeing and VAR in Brazilian football," CBF refereeing director Netto Góes and Refereeing Committee chairman Sandro Meira Ricci discussed the current administration's investments in technology and training to improve the country's refereeing pool. The panel was moderated by Rio Grande do Sul Football Federation president Luciano Hocsman and Luís Otávio Veríssimo, president of the Superior Court of Sports Justice (STJD).

Netto Góes, CBF refereeing directorCredits: Handout

"It is important to talk about what the refereeing department and committee have been doing, but also about the CBF's investment process, which has enabled so many changes in this area. There has been an overhaul of the philosophy and intervention guidelines, and today we are more closely aligned with the STJD, with practices that help Brazilian football run smoothly," he said.

Aline Pellegrino highlighted the importance of discussing improvements to women's football as Brazil prepares to host the Women's World CupCredits: Handout

The development and promotion of women's football were also on the CBF Academy Summit's agenda, with the panel "Building women's football as a product." CBF women's competitions manager Aline Pellegrino highlighted the importance of cooperation among the various stakeholders in Brazilian football at a strategic moment for the women's game, with the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil approaching.

"The Summit is a very important opportunity to bring together the entire Brazilian football ecosystem and address so many topics that can help us move forward. It takes on even greater significance ahead of the Women's World Cup, bringing constructive discussions so that we can deliver a spectacular event worthy of the women's game," Pellegrino said.

#2662. Kalshi daily volume of ‘perps’ trading begins to top its prediction markets

Kalshi is known for its prediction markets across sports, politics and culture.

But now, for the first time, perpetual futures, Kalshi's second financial product, has surpassed the notional trading volume of its event contracts on consecutive days.

On Thursday, perpetual futures — commonly known as "perps" — on Kalshi saw $3.4 billion in notional volume as artificial intelligence laboratory Anthropic stock debuted on public markets while the rest of the market sold off. That exceeded about $3 billion in notional volume for Kalshi's prediction markets on the same day.

Perps are futures-style contracts where there is no expiration and traders do not need to own the underlying asset. Contracts instead continuously track the price of an asset, with funding payments to keep the contract price aligned with that of the market. Funding payments are made periodically between holders of short or long positions.

Perps trading surpassed event contracts one day in September, but on Friday perps topped prediction markets volume for a second day. Now Kalshi expects that performance to continue as it introduces perps tied to more individual stocks. On Monday, for example, Kalshi launched contracts linked to Anthropic.

Kalshi was the first to debut perps in the U.S. after winning federal regulatory approval in May to list perps tied to cryptocurrencies.

Perps trading volume includes any leverage that speculators acquire along with their trade, while event contracts are fully collateralized — for now.

Since the original launch in May, Kalshi has received approval to introduce perps tied to metals, crude oil, stock indexes and individual stocks.

Offshore perps — those available on exchanges not regulated in the U.S. — generated more than $90 trillion in notional trading volume in 2025, so it's not surprising that the product has grown so rapidly on Kalshi, according to Udesh Jha, chief risk officer at Kalshi Klear, the company's clearing house.

"We're just in very early innings. We're launching products, we're growing the participant base."

Perps were Kalshi's first product to mark its transition from a prediction market-focused platform to a full-blown financial exchange where various assets are traded. Last week, reports said that Kalshi is planning to offer trading on equities on its platform in the coming months.

At the same time, the company's perps product has come under fire. Some incumbent exchanges where futures are traded — which saw their stock prices decline following the approval of U.S. perps — believe the product was improperly approved. CME Group is suing the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal derivatives regulator, for approving perps.

Others have simply expressed concerns about the efficiency of the markets. CNBC previously reported that trading volume on Kalshi's most popular perps markets — tied to bitcoin and ether cryptocurrencies — was dramatically greater than open interest, or cash actively in the markets. It's a phenomenon that isn't common with U.S.-regulated traditional futures, nor other offshore perps markets.

Kalshi said at the time it has "zero concerns" about the distinction, and that it appears because less leverage is offered compared to offshore exchanges and there are fewer incentives for traders to park capital on its perps markets.

While Kalshi started with cryptocurrencies, Owen Lau, an analyst at Clear Street, said perps tied to individual stocks likely represent the most promising opportunity for growth in the U.S.

"That's how I foresee the way perps will penetrate further into traditional asset classes," Lau said. "Perps on single stocks and [key performance indicators on individual companies] could change how investors hedge their portfolio or even make a directional bet."

Kalshi's growth has been powered by the fact that right now it's the only exchange that can actively list perps in the U.S., though crypto exchange Coinbase received approval in May to route U.S. users to offshore platforms for trading. That monopoly status, however, will probably prove short lived.

Coinbase has filed to list single-stock perps in the U.S., and President Donald Trump in August said the CFTC is working to bring Hyperliquid — a dominant player in offshore perps activity — to domestic traders.

But Jha at Kalshi isn't worried about the competition.

"What will carry us is ... making sure that we have the right products for the marketplace, making sure we have the right surveillance of the products that we are trading."

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

#2660. Pat Freiermuth: Aaron Rodgers said what he said, I'm focused on Denver

While Aaron Rodgers was going scorched earth on the Steelers and head coach Mike McCarthy during Wednesday's appearance on The Pat McAfee Show, he said that tight end Pat Freiermuth informed him of the team's decision to bench him on Tuesday night.

Rodgers was on the show while the Steelers were practicing, but Freiermuth spoke to reporters in the team's locker room later in the day. #2659. AI debt markets shudder as Nvidia's top 'banker' returns

AI credit markets are shuddering again with Jensen Huang back as CEO of Nvidia.

Fears about the massive debt being taken on to fund the artificial intelligence buildout climbed Tuesday as Wall Street weighed what Huang's return to Nvidia means for its bankrolling of the AI boom.

Huang is considered one of the top financiers, or bankers, in the AI industry, spearheading deals with neoclouds like CoreWeave and other firms to buy chips, backed in some cases by Nvidia guarantees. His return to Nvidia has revived prospects for the company to continue "circular financing" of AI chips and data centers — raising concerns among credit investors.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child of AI debt concerns, saw its stock sink 13% and the yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 top 17%. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

At the same time, the spread on the neocloud company's five-year credit default swaps jumped 8.5% to over 1,200 basis points. Credit default swaps are insurance against nonpayment and are considered a barometer of perceived risks. Rising CDS spreads mean investors view the debt as riskier.

Huang was reinstated as CEO on Monday after stepping down on Nov. 12 amid allegations of multiple affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. His reinstatement on Monday was cheered by investors, who pushed stocks higher, yields lower and spreads on CDS tighter. However, stocks retreated, bond yields rose and CDS spreads widened on Tuesday.

Ben Emons, founder and chief investment officer at FedWatch Advisors, called it a waning of the "Jensen effect."

The moves suggest "markets see government intervention as 'moral suasion' that carries credit and interest-rate risks," he said.

President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday he "convinced" the board to bring Huang back.

CoreWeave wasn't the only name seeing heightened concerns in CDS spreads. Oracle's five-year CDS spread jumped 7% to 355.68. Even highly rated hyperscalers Meta Platforms and Amazon.com saw spreads widen by more than 2%. Nvidia's CDS added 3.4%.

Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds, believes the drama that unfolded with Huang's return to Nvidia won't necessarily sit well with credit investors.

"A lot of old school credit people are going to look at what kind of materialized there, the administration's involvement in putting him back in, and I think a lot of credit participants are going to step back and tiptoe away from that a bit," he said. "Credit market investors typically don't like that type of drama or uncertainty."

While Nvidia has commitments across the AI ecosystem, it is the neoclouds that have been under the most scrutiny. Many of the companies, which rent out AI computing power and cloud capacity, are highly leveraged and have relied on Nvidia financing to reduce their exposure to the bond market.

With so much riding on Nvidia's funding, Huang's next move is being closely watched.

During his brief absence, chief financial officer Colette Kress said during the company's earnings call that Nvidia would be "rigorously evaluating future investments" and will remain disciplined in how it commits capital.

That suggested Nvidia was going to be more judicious with financing, says Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"That concern should be put to rest with Jensen [Huang] back," he said.

Investor Steve Eisman, of "Big Short" fame and host of "The Real Eisman Playbook" podcast, believes Huang feels emboldened now that he's back in charge.

"[H]e'll double down on the circular financing," Eisman predicted on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Tuesday.

After Huang's departure, Eisman believed that the ecosystem the CEO created by pouring money into AI companies would likely unwind and leave some of the companies in "big trouble."

"Now that he's back, they're not," he said.

Others are not so certain the level of funding will continue.

"Given scrutiny of disclosure around financing and guarantees … we do not expect Mr. Huang's return to bring a quick reversion to broader customer financing," Stifel analyst Ruben Roy said in a note Monday.

Nvidia said on its earnings call that it has $118 billion in guarantees, as of Oct. 25, to back AI projects.

Concerns about the level of debt to fund the AI infrastructure buildout had already taken hold before Huang's departure and reinstatement.

"These issues have not disappeared just because the White House pressured the weak board to reinstate Jensen Huang," said economist David Rosenberg, founder and president of Rosenberg Research.

John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson Investors, believes having Huang back at the helm "reaffirms his existing go-to-market strategy." However, the credit market is still taking a cautious look at the neoclouds as it waits for more clarity on long-term supply/demand dynamics.

Still, Lloyd is cautiously positive on CoreWeave, which he owns in portfolios he manages, and noted all the data point to a "pretty healthy environment right now." That includes strong residual values on graphics processing units and spot compute rates, he noted.

"The company is doing everything in its power to execute," he said. "They don't need the high yield market at this time."

In the meantime, investigations into Nvidia and Huang are ramping up. Huang is expected to appear before three House committees next week. Nvidia is conducting an independent investigation into his activities, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta has launched a probe. At the federal level, President Trump said Monday that U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche "has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"There's other shoes to drop," Rosenberg said. "I don't think that the book has been closed on this file."

#2657. Nvidia's billion-dollar board bet: Who's protected as lawsuits mount?

Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia, after President Donald Trump urged the company's board to rehire Huang. But the investigation into the company, its executive leadership and its board continue as outside criticism mounts.

"Clearly they caved to external pressure," said Betsy Atkins, an author and longtime public-company director. "The board failed," she said, when it initially allowed Huang's removal. "The board's role is to think of all stakeholders."

California Attorney General Rob Bonta is investigating whether Nvidia misrepresented information to investors. "There is classic corporate securities law on the books in California that prevents investors and the public from being misled by companies," Bonta said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Tuesday.

Directors are already defendants in a shareholder lawsuit accusing them of failing to oversee Nvidia. A separate securities class action targets the company and Huang, its co-founder.

Now the board’s insurance choices are part of the story. A risk advisor with direct knowledge of Nvidia’s coverage says the company built an approximately $1 billion D&O tower, insurance jargon for directors and officers insurance policies from different companies that combine to cover one massive risk.

Nvidia "loves insurance," the advisor said. “They buy insurance as if they have no balance sheet.” A billion-dollar tower would essentially mean Nvidia "bought the market," purchasing all the coverage it could get, according to an industry expert with 25 years working in financial insurance. The expert asked not to be named out of concern for past or potential future clients.

But Nvidia directed all that coverage to Side A only, according to CNBC's source, which protects directors and officers personally when the company cannot indemnify them. Side B and C leaves Nvidia to bear more of its own risk and legal costs. The risk advisor says Nvidia believed it had "the war chest" to protect itself against a securities class action suit.

That choice is raising questions about whether the board protected itself at the company’s expense. CNBC asked Nvidia for comment but received no response.

An insurance CEO characterized a billion dollar policy as a lot of coverage, but said a Side A-only allocation was a surprising move because it results in imbalanced coverage, protecting only directors.

That structure is not automatically a governance failure, according to a D&O insurance expert with long experience in coverage for banks, drugmakers and other businesses that often face litigation. Side A-only programs are common among companies with the capital to manage the corporate risk internally.

"For a company with Nvidia’s resources, retaining the company-side risk can make financial sense," the adviser said. It's Side A D&O that's "imperative to corporate governance."

"It is a capital-allocation decision," the expert told me. The company decides that buying insurance for its own balance sheet is not worth the premium. In other words, Side B, which covers the company for legal defense costs or settlements on behalf of directors and officers, and Side C, protecting the company when named as a defendant in a suit such as a securities claim, are considered too expensive for the coverage the company gets.

The question for shareholders is whether the board’s decision to hold that risk was a sound use of the company’s resources and whether the company can absorb the costs if the claims grow.

A shareholder derivative complaint filed Nov. 11 names Huang, directors and other officers. It alleges that they failed to oversee risks involving Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang and made misleading statements. It also alleges that some defendants sold roughly $2 billion in Nvidia stock while holding material nonpublic information. Those remain allegations, not findings.

A separate securities class action, filed Nov. 9, names Nvidia and Huang. It seeks damages for investors who bought Nvidia shares between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, alleging the company and Huang misled investors. The distinction matters: the derivative suit is brought on Nvidia’s behalf, while the class action seeks recovery for investors.

"Insurance is already at work," says Michel Léonard, chief economist at the Insurance Information Institute, describing standard policy mechanics, not Nvidia’s specific policy. "Once the suit is filed, D&O starts paying defense costs, long before anyone proves anything."

A claim still has to meet the policy’s terms, and defense costs can reduce the remaining limits. Nor does a drop in Nvidia’s market value by itself establish an insurable loss. Plaintiffs would need to prove legally recoverable damages; the policy would respond only to covered losses.

The board has already taken steps it says are aimed at accountability. Nvidia announced an independent investigation on Nov. 8, and independent directors retained outside counsel two days later. Huang resigned as CEO and a director on Nov. 11; the board appointed CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. Nvidia said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised by Huang's extramarital relationships.

Atkins, who joined the board of Wynn Resorts in 2018 after founder Steve Wynn resigned, argues that allegations are not conclusions and that boards should also weigh governance concerns against the value a founder brings to a company’s innovation. Nvidia's investigation is continuing even as Huang resumes leadership.

“Will companies’ hyper-accelerated innovation speed be the same without them? I don’t think so,” said Atkins, author of Don't Waste a Board Seat: A Decision-Maker's Guide to Choosing Directors Who Create Value.

Nvidia’s 2026 proxy also says the company has indemnity agreements with its directors and officers — separate from its insurance. Those agreements provide for the company to cover certain costs and liabilities when the law permits.

Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers reacts at a news conference. AP Photo/Chris Szagola
